"'''I Love You Always Forever'''" is a song by Welsh singer [[Donna Lewis]] from her debut album, ''[[Now in a Minute]]'' (1996). Written by Lewis and produced by Lewis and Kevin Killen, it was released as the album's [[lead single]]. In the United States, it was serviced to [[contemporary hit radio]] on 16 April 1996 and was issued commercially on 7 May, while in the United Kingdom, it was released on 26 August. The song is inspired by [[H. E. Bates]]' novel ''[[Love for Lydia]]'', from which the chorus is taken.<ref name="spokesman"/>

The song was a commercial hit, peaking at number five on the [[UK Singles Chart]] and reaching the top 10 in more than 15 countries, including Australia, Austria, Canada, France, Ireland, and Norway. In the US, the song rose to number two on the [[Billboard (magazine)|''Billboard'']] [[Billboard Hot 100|Hot 100]], where it remained for nine weeks, behind [[Los del Río]]'s "[[Macarena (song)|Macarena]]". It was [[Music recording certification|certified]] platinum in Australia and the UK and gold in France, Germany, New Zealand, Norway, and the US. The accompanying music video was directed by Randee St. Nicholas. The success of the song saw Lewis nominated for the [[Brit Awards|Brit Award]] for [[Brit Award for British Female Solo Artist|Best British Female Artist]] in 1997.<ref name="BRIT Nom">[http://www.brits.co.uk/artist/donna-lewis Donna Lewis BRITS Profile] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130216064849/http://www.brits.co.uk/artist/donna-lewis |date=16 February 2013 }}. BRIT Awards Ltd. Retrieved 26 January 2013</ref> In 2023, ''Billboard'' ranked "I Love You Always Forever" among the "500 Best Pop Songs of All Time".<ref name="billboard500bestpopsongs">{{cite magazine|url=https://www.billboard.com/lists/best-pop-songs-all-time-hits/donna-lewis-i-love-you-always-forever/|title=The 500 Best Pop Songs: Staff List|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]|date=19 October 2023|access-date=20 October 2023}}</ref>

In 2016, a cover version of the song by Australian pop singer [[Betty Who]] peaked at number six on the [[ARIA Singles Chart]] and topped the US ''Billboard'' [[Dance Club Songs]] chart.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c9E8nBJWfSY|title=Betty Who - I Love You Always Forever (Audio)|author=BettyWhoVEVO|via=YouTube|date=3 June 2016|url-status=live|archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211213/c9E8nBJWfSY|archive-date=13 December 2021}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

"I Love You Always Forever" is a song by Welsh singer Donna Lewis from her debut album, Now in a Minute (1996). Written by Lewis and produced by Lewis and Kevin Killen, it was released as the album's lead single. In the United States, it was serviced to contemporary hit radio on 16 April 1996 and was issued commercially on 7 May, while in the United Kingdom, it was released on 26 August. The song is inspired by H. E. Bates' novel Love for Lydia, from which the chorus is taken.

The song was a commercial hit, peaking at number five on the UK Singles Chart and reaching the top 10 in more than 15 countries, including Australia, Austria, Canada, France, Ireland, and Norway. In the US, the song rose to number two on the Billboard Hot 100, where it remained for nine weeks, behind Los del Río's "Macarena". It was certified platinum in Australia and the UK and gold in France, Germany, New Zealand, Norway, and the US. The accompanying music video was directed by Randee St. Nicholas. The success of the song saw Lewis nominated for the Brit Award for Best British Female Artist in 1997. In 2023, Billboard ranked "I Love You Always Forever" among the "500 Best Pop Songs of All Time".

In 2016, a cover version of the song by Australian pop singer Betty Who peaked at number six on the ARIA Singles Chart and topped the US Billboard Dance Club Songs chart.

sections.heading: Background
sections.wikitext: Inspired by the novel ''[[Love for Lydia]]'' by [[H. E. Bates]], "I Love You Always Forever" is a pop song in which the singer declares her endless love for her significant other. The song was originally titled "Lydia", but was later changed because there was no mention of anyone with that name in the song. The chorus, "I love you always forever, near and far closer together", is a quote taken directly from the book.<ref name="spokesman">{{cite web|last1=Crowe|first1=Jerry|title=Runner Up Donna Lewis' 'I Love You Always Forever' Is Stuck at No. 2 on Billboard Chart Behind A Certain Dance Song|date=16 October 1996|url=http://www.spokesman.com/stories/1996/oct/16/runner-up-donna-lewis-i-love-you-always-forever/|website=The Spokesman-Review|access-date=25 November 2016}}</ref>
sections.text: Inspired by the novel Love for Lydia by H. E. Bates, "I Love You Always Forever" is a pop song in which the singer declares her endless love for her significant other. The song was originally titled "Lydia", but was later changed because there was no mention of anyone with that name in the song. The chorus, "I love you always forever, near and far closer together", is a quote taken directly from the book.

sections.heading: Composition
sections.wikitext: "I Love You Always Forever" is written in the key of [[C major]] in [[Time signature|common time]] with a [[tempo]] of 104 beats per minute.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://songbpm.com/@donna-lewis/i-love-you-always-forever|title=Donna Lewis - I Love You Always Forever|website=songbpm.com|access-date=23 August 2018}}</ref>{{Verify source|date=November 2022}} Lewis' vocals span from F<sub>3</sub> to G<sub>4</sub> in the song.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.musicnotes.com/sheetmusic/mtd.asp?ppn=MN0090015|title=Donna Lewis "I Love You Always Forever" Sheet Music in C Major (transposable) - Download & Print|last=Lewis|first=Donna|website=Musicnotes.com|access-date=4 August 2016}}</ref>

sections.heading: Reception
sections.wikitext:
The success of "I Love You Always Forever" earned Lewis a nomination for [[Brit Award for British Female Solo Artist|Best British Female Artist]] at the [[Brit Awards 1997|1997 Brit Awards]].<ref name="BRIT Nom"/> In the US, Andrea Ganis, executive VP of Lewis' record label, [[Atlantic Records|Atlantic]], said: "Radio stations across the country keep telling us the same thing over and over", Ganis says. "They play it and, almost overnight, it's their most requested song. Maybe it's because things have been so dark lately in pop and then along comes a record that everybody can sing along to. It's almost like a catharsis for a lot of people."<ref name="spokesman"/> It became a "runaway hit" without any extra marketing boost from high-profile events of the time such as a hit movie or the [[1996 Atlanta Olympic Games]], and was the first single to achieve over one million airplay detections in the US.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hiponline.com/1951/donna-lewis.html|title=Donna Lewis|website=hiponlline.com|date=14 February 2008|access-date=9 April 2019}}</ref>

[[AllMusic]] editor Tom Demalon called the song "compelling" in his review of ''[[Now in a Minute]]''. He noted that Lewis "has a girlish voice that sounds like a less quirky [[Kate Bush]]."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.allmusic.com/album/now-in-a-minute-mw0000183466|title=Donna Lewis - Now in a Minute|publisher=[[AllMusic]]|access-date=19 March 2020}}</ref> [[Larry Flick]] from ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' magazine described it as a "quietly percussive pop chugger", complimenting Lewis' voice as a "delicate, girlish voice that gives the song a winsome quality, which adds to its already considerable charm."<ref>{{cite magazine|first=Larry|last=Flick|url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/90s/1996/BB-1996-05-18.pdf|title=Single Reviews|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]|date=18 May 1996|access-date=5 February 2020|page=70|author-link=Larry Flick}}</ref> Tracey Pepper from ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'' noted that it is "more sophisticated than a first listen might reveal. "I Love You Always Forever"'s chanted chorus, chugging rhythm, and bright melody make it obvious that the newcomer Donna Lewis, whose girlish voice often sounds like [[Cyndi Lauper]]'s, knows the value of building tension and mood, even in a pop song."<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://ew.com/article/1996/08/09/i-love-you-always-forever/|title=I Love You Always Forever|magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]]|date=9 August 1996|access-date=27 February 2020}}</ref> Eamon Joyce from ''[[Miscellany News]]'' commented that "upon hearing the song, it's embedded in your head for weeks."<ref>{{cite magazine|first= Eamon |last= Joyce |title= QUICK CLIPS |magazine= [[Miscellany News]] |date= 8 November 1996 |page= 13 |access-date= 28 April 2020 |url= https://news.hrvh.org/veridian/cgi-bin/senylrc?a=d&d=vcmisc19961108-01.2.42}}</ref> Bob Waliszewski of ''[[Focus on the Family|Plugged In]]'' stated that Lewis "pledges lifelong commitment" on the song.<ref>{{cite web|first= Bob |last= Waliszewski |title= Now in a Minute |work= Plugged In |publisher= [[Focus on the Family]] |access-date= 27 March 2020 |url= https://www.pluggedin.com/album-reviews/donnalewis-nowinaminute/}}</ref>
sections.text:
The success of "I Love You Always Forever" earned Lewis a nomination for Best British Female Artist at the 1997 Brit Awards. In the US, Andrea Ganis, executive VP of Lewis' record label, Atlantic, said: "Radio stations across the country keep telling us the same thing over and over", Ganis says. "They play it and, almost overnight, it's their most requested song. Maybe it's because things have been so dark lately in pop and then along comes a record that everybody can sing along to. It's almost like a catharsis for a lot of people." It became a "runaway hit" without any extra marketing boost from high-profile events of the time such as a hit movie or the 1996 Atlanta Olympic Games, and was the first single to achieve over one million airplay detections in the US.

AllMusic editor Tom Demalon called the song "compelling" in his review of Now in a Minute. He noted that Lewis "has a girlish voice that sounds like a less quirky Kate Bush." Larry Flick from Billboard magazine described it as a "quietly percussive pop chugger", complimenting Lewis' voice as a "delicate, girlish voice that gives the song a winsome quality, which adds to its already considerable charm." Tracey Pepper from Entertainment Weekly noted that it is "more sophisticated than a first listen might reveal. "I Love You Always Forever"'s chanted chorus, chugging rhythm, and bright melody make it obvious that the newcomer Donna Lewis, whose girlish voice often sounds like Cyndi Lauper's, knows the value of building tension and mood, even in a pop song." Eamon Joyce from Miscellany News commented that "upon hearing the song, it's embedded in your head for weeks." Bob Waliszewski of Plugged In stated that Lewis "pledges lifelong commitment" on the song.

sections.heading: Music video
sections.wikitext: The music video for "I Love You Always Forever" was directed by Randee St. Nicholas.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ka1c1qOd0Es|title=Donna Lewis - I Love You Always Forever (Viva TV Köln)|publisher=[[YouTube]]|accessdate=27 January 2026}} See information in the video.</ref> It is very simple, showing Lewis performing the song dressed in all white in a beige rotating room. Other scenes feature her against a black background, with snow boots on her hands against a wall, and playing a piano.

sections.heading: Impact and legacy
sections.wikitext: ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' magazine ranked "I Love You Always Forever" number 408 in their list of "500 Best Pop Songs of All Time" in October 2023,<ref name="billboard500bestpopsongs" /> writing, "The gauziest pop smash of the mid-’90s, as soft and billowing and comforting as the fuzzy curtains Donna Lewis surrounds herself with in the song’s music video." [[Insider Inc.|Insider]] featured the song in their "The 51 Best Love Songs of All Time" in 2018. Kim Renfro added that it is a "true bop" that is reminiscent of Cyndi Lauper's music of 10 years earlier, but with "slightly more pizazz".<ref>{{cite web|last=Renfro|first=Kim|url=https://www.thisisinsider.com/best-love-songs-ranked-2018-5|title=RANKED: The 51 best love songs of all time|publisher=[[Insider Inc.|Insider]]|date=16 May 2018|access-date=7 April 2019}}</ref> Same year, ''Stacker'' ranked it number ten in their list of "Best Pop Songs of the Last 25 years", noting Lewis' "ethereal voice over a heavenly backdrop of synthesizers and understated drum beats".<ref>{{cite web|first=Jacob|last=Osborn|title=Best pop songs of the last 25 years|publisher=Stacker|url=https://thestacker.com/stories/1500/best-pop-songs-last-25-years#42|date=29 August 2018|access-date=22 April 2020}}</ref>

sections.heading: Other releases
sections.wikitext: Lewis has re-recorded the song at least twice. A re-recording with slightly modified instrumentation appears as a bonus track of her 2008 album ''[[In the Pink (Donna Lewis album)|In the Pink]]''. In 2015, Lewis released the song again on her jazz-influenced covers album, ''[[Donna Lewis#Discography|Brand New Day]]''. She was reluctant to include the song at all; but the track that appears on the album has a "completely different arrangement", and Lewis says she now likes it.<ref>{{cite web|last=Heigl|url=https://people.com/celebrity/donna-lewis-i-love-you-always-forever-singers-new-album/|title=Interview: Donna Lewis's Brand New Day|magazine=[[People (magazine)|People]]|date=9 March 2015|access-date=7 April 2019}}</ref> Matt Collar of [[AllMusic]] felt that the new version was a "ruminative reworking" of the original.<ref>{{cite web|last=Collar|first=Matt|url=https://www.allmusic.com/album/brand-new-day-mw0002814373|title=Donna Lewis - Brand New Day|website=AllMusic|access-date=7 April 2019}}</ref>
sections.text: Lewis has re-recorded the song at least twice. A re-recording with slightly modified instrumentation appears as a bonus track of her 2008 album In the Pink. In 2015, Lewis released the song again on her jazz-influenced covers album, Brand New Day. She was reluctant to include the song at all; but the track that appears on the album has a "completely different arrangement", and Lewis says she now likes it. Matt Collar of AllMusic felt that the new version was a "ruminative reworking" of the original.

Australian pop singer Betty Who released a version of the song on 3 June 2016, with remixes released on 29 July 2016. It was released as the lead single from her second studio album, The Valley.

sections.heading: Music video
sections.wikitext: The music video, directed by Ben Cope and Daniel Gomes, was released on 14 July 2016.
sections.text: The music video, directed by Ben Cope and Daniel Gomes, was released on 14 July 2016.

sections.heading: Chart performance
sections.wikitext: The song was Who's first to enter the Australian [[ARIA Singles Chart]], peaking at number six, while also reaching number one on AirCheck's National Radio Airplay Chart. The song has also had minor success in New Zealand, peaking at number 33. The song was successful on the US [[Dance Club Songs]] chart, where it peaked at number one, becoming her third number one on the chart.
sections.text: The song was Who's first to enter the Australian ARIA Singles Chart, peaking at number six, while also reaching number one on AirCheck's National Radio Airplay Chart. The song has also had minor success in New Zealand, peaking at number 33. The song was successful on the US Dance Club Songs chart, where it peaked at number one, becoming her third number one on the chart.
